claims.text: Lower grain-boundary/interface density enhances the high-temperature structural stability of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Lower grain-boundary/interface density enhances the high-temperature chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Reducing interfacial area reduces pathways for rapid diffusion.
Reducing interfacial area suppresses elemental segregation.
Elemental segregation can trigger phase transformations in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Increasing grain size decreases grain-boundary/interface density.
Grain boundaries and interfacial regions act as accelerated diffusion pathways.
Grain boundaries and interfacial regions act as nucleation sites for secondary phases.
Fine-grained nanoalloys undergo faster interface-mediated diffusion than coarse-grained nanoalloys.
High interface density promotes segregation or nucleation of destabilizing phases.
A coarse-grained microstructure limits diffusion-driven segregation and phase nucleation, thereby preserving structural and chemical stability.
After identical high-temperature exposure, larger-grained samples will exhibit less grain growth than fine-grained samples.
After identical high-temperature exposure, larger-grained samples will exhibit less phase segregation than fine-grained samples.
After identical high-temperature exposure, larger-grained samples will exhibit fewer signs of chemical instability than fine-grained samples.
The effect of grain-boundary density on stability is expected to be most important during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
At lower temperatures or short exposure times, the influence of grain-boundary density on stability may be negligible.
Interfacial diffusion is expected to dominate stability relative to intrinsic configurational entropy.
The relative contribution of interfacial diffusion and configurational entropy may vary with elemental makeup and testing temperature.
